title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Jul 21, 2026
intro: This edition is about agent infrastructure: sandbox agents so a compromised run can't spread, turn migrations into a loop instead of a file-by-file slog, and dial retrieval, evals, and reasoning effort to cut cost without cutting reliability.

cards.title: Proxy GitHub tokens instead of handing agents your real PAT
cards.problem: An agent that runs `gh` needs a token in its environment, and any sandboxed process holding a real PAT can leak or misuse it.
cards.apply: Export a dummy `GH_TOKEN` inside the sandbox so the CLI's local auth check passes, then run an egress proxy in front of the sandbox that swaps in the real PAT only on outbound requests — `Bearer` auth for `api.github.com`, base64 `Basic` auth for `github.com` git operations.
cards.result: The author reports the real credential never enters the sandbox, so a compromised or misbehaving agent process has nothing to exfiltrate.

evidence.note: Author describes the egress-proxy architecture they built and its security property; no independent measurement.

cards.title: Give each agent task its own microVM, not a shared dev container
cards.problem: Agent-written code often executes before a human reviews it, and a shared container can't fully isolate that risk from your other work.
cards.apply: Run each agent task in its own hardware-virtualized microVM with an independent kernel and filesystem, inject credentials via proxy instead of baking them into the image, and use snapshot-and-fork so parallel fix attempts branch from one base image without sharing state.
cards.result: LangChain reports that what runs in one microVM can't affect what runs in another, so a broken or compromised agent run stays contained to itself.

evidence.note: Vendor blog describing their own sandboxing product architecture and its isolation guarantee.

cards.title: Fix the loop that produces migration code, not the files it outputs
cards.problem: Hand-patching agent-translated files one at a time doesn't scale past a few hundred files, and the same mistake keeps recurring across them.
cards.apply: Write a rulebook and dependency map first, stress-test it on a small subset, then run parallel agents (a smaller model to translate, a larger model to review) against compile-test-verify gates; when reviewers spot a repeated mistake, add one line to the rulebook and regenerate instead of hand-fixing individual files.
cards.result: Anthropic used this loop to port Bun's ~1 million-line Zig codebase to Rust in under two weeks, passing 100% of the existing test suite with only 19 post-merge regressions.

evidence.note: Anthropic reports measured test-pass rate, regression count, token spend, and performance deltas from the Bun migration.

cards.title: Run agent retrieval on Postgres instead of a dedicated vector DB
cards.problem: A separate vector database adds a second system to operate, and it still can't give an agent deterministic relational context alongside semantic search.
cards.apply: Use Postgres's own JSONB indexing for semi-structured payloads, an HNSW index (not IVFFLAT) for embeddings, and quantize vectors from 32-bit floats to 8- or 16-bit; give agents high-level DB tools plus row-level access control instead of raw SQL.
cards.result: One system covers both deterministic relational queries and semantic retrieval, and the source reports quantization alone delivers a 4x improvement in memory, disk, and CPU cost.

evidence.note: Speaker cites a specific measured 4x resource-cost improvement from vector quantization.

cards.title: Take the central datastore out of your sandbox-creation path
cards.problem: Centralized scheduling that serializes sandbox creation and writes O(sandboxes) database rows per request tips over long before you reach real agent-fleet scale.
cards.apply: Run horizontally-scaled schedulers as stateless load balancers, let each worker be its own source of truth publishing state asynchronously to Redis instead of a central datastore, and batch control messages instead of sending one RPC per sandbox.
cards.result: Modal reports creating 1 million concurrent sandboxes in under 60 seconds, with median creation-to-interactive latency under 500ms and no latency degradation as scale increases.

evidence.note: Modal published its own load-test benchmark numbers for the new scheduler.

cards.title: Score agents on multi-turn traces, not single-shot benchmarks
cards.problem: Static single-turn benchmarks miss the failure modes that only show up once an agent holds state across a long session.
cards.apply: Build eval infrastructure around multi-turn conversation traces and simulation feedback loops, and pair it with harness-level controls — own the state, order the mutations, require an audit trail before an action executes — instead of relying on prompt-level guardrails alone.
cards.result: Teams treating evals as ongoing infrastructure catch state-mutation bugs and unsafe tool calls that single-turn tests structurally can't see.

evidence.note: Synthesized from multiple QCon AI Boston talks on eval and harness design; no single measured benchmark to cite.

cards.title: Set reasoning effort per call type instead of one global setting
cards.problem: Running every agent call at maximum reasoning effort burns tokens on steps where extra reasoning barely moves accuracy.
cards.apply: Set an explicit low/medium/high reasoning-effort level per call type instead of one global setting — reserve high effort for tasks where the accuracy gap over medium is real, and default routine tool-calling or classification steps to medium or low.
cards.result: The piece reports medium effort typically holds 85-95% of max-effort benchmark performance at 50-70% of the token cost, and that Kimi K2.5's effort toggle cut tokens 25-30% with little accuracy change.

evidence.note: Cites specific benchmark performance-retention and token-reduction figures reported for GPT-5.6/gpt-oss and Kimi K2.5.
